metadata.title: CIS Docker Benchmark — Security Best Practices

entries.description: Never run a container as root (UID 0). Create a dedicated user and group in the Dockerfile. Example: groupadd --gid 1001 appgroup && useradd --uid 1001 --gid appgroup --no-create-home appuser, then USER appuser before CMD.
decision_rules: Always add a non-root user in the Dockerfile before the CMD/ENTRYPOINT instruction
Use fixed UID/GID (e.g. 1001) to ensure consistent file ownership across image rebuilds
tradeoffs: Some applications require root for initialization — use gosu or tini as entrypoint wrappers to drop privileges after init
anti_patterns: Running containers without a USER directive (defaults to root)
Using USER root explicitly in production images
aws_alignment: ECS task definitions should set user in containerDefinitions
EKS pod specs should set runAsNonRoot: true in securityContext

entries.description: Mount the container filesystem as read-only to prevent unauthorized runtime modifications. In docker-compose: read_only: true with tmpfs mounts for /tmp and /var/run. CLI equivalent: docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp myapp:latest.
decision_rules: Enable read_only: true for all stateless services
Add tmpfs mounts for directories requiring write access at runtime (e.g. /tmp, /var/run)
tradeoffs: Application must not write to the container filesystem — may require refactoring logging or temp file paths
anti_patterns: Running containers with writable root filesystem in production
Not providing tmpfs for required write paths when read-only is enabled
aws_alignment: Map to readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in ECS containerDefinitions
Map to readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in Kubernetes securityContext

entries.description: Start by dropping all Linux capabilities (cap_drop: ALL), then add back only those strictly required (e.g. cap_add: NET_BIND_SERVICE if the service listens on a port below 1024).
decision_rules: Apply cap_drop: [ALL] as the baseline for every container
Add back only specific capabilities required by the application — document the reason
tradeoffs: Identifying required capabilities may take experimentation; run container with strace or auditd to detect capability use
anti_patterns: Running containers without capability restrictions
Adding broad capabilities (SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN) without justification

entries.description: Always define memory and CPU limits to prevent a single container from causing Denial of Service. In docker-compose deploy.resources: limits memory 512m cpus 0.5, reservations memory 128m cpus 0.1.
decision_rules: Set both memory limits and CPU limits for all production containers
Define reservations (requests) in addition to limits to enable proper scheduling
tradeoffs: Limits that are too tight cause OOM kills or CPU throttling — profile the application before setting values
anti_patterns: Deploying containers with no memory or CPU limits to shared hosts
Setting limits without reservations — scheduler cannot guarantee resource availability
aws_alignment: Map to memory and cpu in ECS task definition resource requirements
Map to resources.requests and resources.limits in Kubernetes pod spec

entries.description: Never use privileged: true in production. Privileged containers have full access to the host kernel. Use security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true] to prevent privilege escalation.
decision_rules: Set security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true] on all containers
Reject any deployment manifest that sets privileged: true without explicit documented justification
tradeoffs: Some monitoring or networking tools require privileged mode — isolate them in dedicated namespaces with extra controls
anti_patterns: Setting privileged: true for application containers
Using privileged mode as a workaround for missing capabilities

entries.description: Attach a seccomp profile (seccomp:seccomp-profile.json) and AppArmor profile (apparmor:docker-default) via security_opt to restrict the system calls available to the container.
decision_rules: Use the docker-default AppArmor profile as a minimum baseline
Use the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile in Kubernetes (seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault)
tradeoffs: Custom seccomp profiles require profiling the application's syscall usage first
AppArmor is Linux-specific — not applicable on Windows containers
anti_patterns: Running containers with unconfined seccomp (--security-opt seccomp=unconfined)
Disabling AppArmor profiles for production containers

entries.concept: Use minimal base images to reduce attack surface
entries.description: Prefer distroless (no shell, no package manager) or alpine (~5 MB) base images. Distroless example: gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12. Alpine example: python:3.11-alpine. Fewer packages means fewer CVEs.
decision_rules: Default to *-slim variants when distroless is not feasible
Use distroless for production runtime stages in multi-stage builds
Run image scanners after every build to detect new CVEs
tradeoffs: Distroless images have no shell — debugging requires ephemeral debug containers (kubectl debug)
Alpine uses musl libc — some Python packages may not have compatible wheels
anti_patterns: Using ubuntu:latest or debian:latest as a base image for production containers
Not updating base images regularly — stale images accumulate CVEs
aws_alignment: ECR image scanning with Snyk/Trivy should be enabled for all repositories

entries.concept: Scan images for vulnerabilities before deployment
entries.description: Use vulnerability scanners on every image before pushing or deploying. Tools: Trivy (trivy image myapp:latest --severity CRITICAL,HIGH), Grype (grype myapp:latest), Docker Scout (docker scout cves myapp:latest).
decision_rules: Gate CI/CD pipeline on Trivy or Grype scan results — fail on CRITICAL severity
Scan both the application image and the base image separately
tradeoffs: Scanning adds 1-5 minutes to CI pipeline — acceptable for security assurance
Scanners may produce false positives — triage HIGH findings before blocking
anti_patterns: Deploying images without any vulnerability scan
Ignoring CRITICAL CVEs in scanner output without documented risk acceptance
aws_alignment: Enable Amazon ECR enhanced scanning (Inspector-based) for automatic push-time scanning

entries.concept: Never embed secrets in Docker images (CIS 4.10)
entries.description: Do not use ENV to set secrets (e.g. ENV API_KEY=sk-secret123). Use Docker BuildKit secrets (RUN --mount=type=secret,id=api_key) or inject secrets at runtime via environment variables from a vault or secrets manager.
decision_rules: Reject any Dockerfile with ENV instructions containing passwords, tokens, or API keys
Use RUN --mount=type=secret for secrets needed only during build time (e.g. pip install from private registry)
tradeoffs: BuildKit secret mounts require Docker BuildKit enabled (DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1)
anti_patterns: ENV API_KEY=sk-secret123 in Dockerfile — secret is visible in image history
ARG SECRET=default_value — visible in build logs and image metadata
aws_alignment: Inject secrets from AWS Secrets Manager at container startup via ECS secrets configuration
Use Parameter Store or Secrets Manager references in ECS task definitions

entries.description: A comprehensive .dockerignore prevents secrets and unnecessary files from being added to the build context. Should exclude: .env, .env.*, *.pem, *.key, *.p12, secrets/, .git/, __pycache__/, *.pyc, node_modules/, .DS_Store.
decision_rules: Always include a .dockerignore in every project with a Dockerfile
Exclude all secret files, credentials, and VCS metadata from the build context
tradeoffs: Over-aggressive .dockerignore may exclude files needed for the build — review carefully
anti_patterns: Not having a .dockerignore — risks accidentally copying .env or private keys into the image
Copying the entire repository context without filtering out secrets
